threads.body: These points are expected to only have the `state` attribute (see `SystemMetrics` recording with fixed `Attributes.of(state, ...)`). Using `hasAttributesSatisfying(...)` will still pass if unexpected extra attributes are added later. Consider switching to an exact attribute assertion (`hasAttributesSatisfyingExactly(...)` or `hasAttributes(...)`) so the test will catch unintended attribute changes.

threads.body: In the `system.memory.utilization` assertions, `isPositive()` requires both `state=used` and `state=free` values to be strictly > 0. But `SystemMetrics` computes these as fractions of total memory, so either value can legitimately be 0.0 (e.g., available==total => used==0.0, or available==0 => free==0.0). To avoid a flaky/incorrect test, consider asserting the values are within [0, 1] (or at least non-negative) instead of strictly positive.

threads.body: `ProcessMetrics` records points using `Attributes.of(TYPE_KEY, ...)`, so point attributes should be exactly `{type=rss}` / `{type=vms}` (and similarly for cpu_time). Using `hasAttributesSatisfying(...)` will not fail if extra unexpected attributes are added. Consider using an exact attribute assertion (`hasAttributesSatisfyingExactly(...)` or `hasAttributes(...)`) to make the tests more regression-sensitive.

threads.body: In the `system.memory.usage` test, the two `hasPointsSatisfying(...)` consumers only assert point attributes, and the subsequent `anySatisfy(... isPositive())` can still pass even if the `state=used` point is negative (e.g., if `mem.getAvailable() > mem.getTotal()` leads to `total-available < 0`). Consider asserting each point’s value is non-negative directly in the point consumers (e.g., `hasValueSatisfying(v -> v.isNotNegative())` for both `used` and `free`) and then dropping the separate `anySatisfy(isPositive())` check (since 0 is valid).
